prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
High-dimensional data assimilation—correcting model predictions with real-world observations—is critical for complex physical systems like weather forecasting or fluid dynamics. While recent generative approaches, specifically Ensemble Score Filters (EnSF), have shown promise in handling high-dimensional non-linear systems, they face a critical failure mode when dealing with **sparse observations**.

In scenarios where sensors are scarce (e.g., measuring ocean wave height at only a few points in a vast grid), the standard score-based update breaks down. The intuition behind this failure is the "vanishing gradient" problem: EnSF relies on the gradient of the log-likelihood to guide the diffusion process toward the true state. When observations are spatially sparse, this gradient is zero almost everywhere (in the unobserved regions). Consequently, the filter cannot effectively propagate information from the sparse observation points to the rest of the state, rendering the assimilation ineffective.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can overcome the sparsity limitation by shifting the assimilation process from the high-dimensional physical space to a compressed **latent manifold**.

Our core intuition is that while observations may be sparse in physical space, they can be mapped to a dense representation in a latent space that is consistent with the latent representation of the full physical state. By aligning the latent encodings of "full states" and "sparse observations," we effectively convert a sparse filtering problem into a dense one. We posit that performing score-based diffusion in this shared latent space will insure non-vanishing gradients, allowing the particle filter to update the global state efficiently based on limited local data.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to develop a method named "Latent-EnSF." The approach consists of two distinct phases: a representation learning phase (Coupled VAE) and a latent filtering phase.

**1. Coupled Variational Autoencoder (VAE) Architecture**
We will design a specialized VAE architecture to bridge the gap between full system states and sparse sensor data.
*   **Dual Encoders:** We will utilize two separate neural network encoders. The *State Encoder* will map the full, high-dimensional physical state into a lower-dimensional latent distribution. The *Observation Encoder* will map the sparse, incomplete observation vector into the *same* latent space.
*   **Shared Decoder:** A single decoder will learn to reconstruct the full physical state from latent samples.
*   **Latent Alignment Strategy:** During training, we will enforce a consistency constraint. We will optimize the networks not just for reconstruction, but to ensure that the latent representation of a sparse observation matches the latent representation of the corresponding full state. This effectively forces the network to "fill in the blanks" during the encoding process.

**2. Latent Space Data Assimilation**
Once the representation is learned, the filtering process will occur entirely within the latent space:
*   **Latent Dynamics:** We will project the physical system dynamics into the latent space (or approximate them if an explicit model is unavailable).
*   **Dense Likelihood Update:** We will apply the Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) to the latent variables. Because the Observation Encoder maps sparse data to a dense latent vector that is aligned with the state, the "latent observation map" effectively becomes an identity function.
*   **Score-Based Diffusion:** We will solve the reverse-time stochastic differential equation (diffusion) to sample from the posterior distribution. Crucially, because the latent observation is dense, the score function (gradient of the likelihood) will be non-zero and informative, guiding the ensemble members correctly.
*   **State Recovery:** Finally, the updated latent particles will be passed through the decoder to obtain the corrected high-dimensional physical states.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Advancement:** This work will extend the applicability of score-based generative filtering (EnSF) to the regime of sparse data, solving the vanishing gradient problem inherent in current diffusion-based assimilation methods.
*   **Computational Efficiency:** By performing the expensive filtering steps in a reduced-order latent space rather than the high-dimensional physical space, we expect to significantly reduce computational costs and wall-clock time.
*   **Robustness:** The coupled encoding strategy offers a way to handle extreme sparsity (e.g., highly scattered sensors) without relying on traditional localization heuristics that often introduce bias in non-linear systems.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

### Shallow Water Wave Propagation (Synthetic)
*   **Physical Model:** Shallow-water equations (hyperbolic PDEs for free-surface fluid flow) modeling water height and two velocity components.
*   **Domain:** Square domain $L \times L$ ($L = 10^6$ m) with constant depth $h = 100$ m.
*   **Discretization:** Uniform $150 \times 150$ grid ($d = 22,500$ per variable).
*   **Simulation Parameters:** 
    *   Time steps: 2000.
    *   Scheme: Upwind scheme.
    *   Time step size: $\Delta t = 0.1 \Delta x / \sqrt{gh}$ where $\Delta x = L/150$.
*   **Initial Conditions:** 
    *   True state: Local Gaussian bump perturbation from a flat surface.
    *   Assimilation initialization: Gaussian bump perturbation shifted away from the true initial state, with added noise to generate the ensemble.
*   **Observation Sparsity:** 
    *   Tested reduction factors: $4\times$ ($75 \times 75$ grid) and $225\times$ ($10 \times 10$ grid).
    *   Temporal sparsity: Observations assimilated every $k$ simulation steps (default $k=20$; tested 5, 20, 50).
*   **Model Architecture (VAE):** 
    *   Input dimension: $3 \times 150 \times 150$.
    *   Encoder: Convolutional layers.
    *   Latent dimension: $400$ ($4 \times 10 \times 10$ with 4 channels).
*   **Latent Noise Handling:** Heuristic approximation using mean standard deviation of encoded latent states; scaling parameter $\psi_{\text{latent}} = 20$.
*   **Ensemble Size:** 100 samples (default). Tested 20 and 1000 for specific EnSF baselines.
*   **Sampling:** 100 forward Euler steps for reverse-time SDE.

### Medium-Range Weather Forecasting (Real-World)
*   **Dataset:** ERA5 (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts).
    *   Training/Testing split: 10 years of data.
    *   Variables: 21 variables (matching FourCastNet configuration).
    *   Resolution: $2.5^\circ$ ($144 \times 72$ grid).
*   **Dynamical Model:** FourCastNet (ML-based prediction model) trained on the coarse subset.
*   **Model Architecture (VAE):** 
    *   ResNet-style architecture.
    *   Encoder downsampling factor: 4.
    *   Latent dimension: $20,736$ ($32 \times 36 \times 18$).
*   **Assimilation Schedule:** Once per day.
*   **Observation Sparsity:** $64\times$ reduction ($18 \times 9$ grid).
*   **Evaluation Protocol:** Metrics averaged across nine 41-day windows.

### Evaluation Metrics
*   **Accuracy:** Relative Root Mean Square Error (RMSE).
*   **Efficiency:** Wall-clock time (seconds per assimilation step).

### Hardware
*   **GPU:** Nvidia A6000.
*   **CPU:** AMD 7543.

### Baselines Compared
*   **EnSF:** Ensemble Score Filter (in full state space).
*   **Latent-EnKF:** Ensemble Kalman Filter operating in the shared VAE latent space.
*   **Latent-LETKF:** Localized Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter operating in the shared VAE latent space (parallelized with 64 cores).
*   **Vanilla LETKF:** Standard LETKF.
*   **FourCastNet (No DA):** Pure ML forecasting without data assimilation.
*   **Latent-EnSF No Model:** Latent-EnSF assuming static dynamics ($x_{t+1} = x_t$).

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Computational Efficiency (Mean and Standard Deviation of Wall-Clock Time in Seconds)**
| Dataset | Latent Dimension | Latent-EnKF (Time in s) | Latent-LETKF (Time in s) | Latent-EnSF (Time in s) | EnSF (Time in s) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| SWE | 400 | 0.056 ± 0.002 | 0.103 ± 0.001 | 0.051 ± 0.001 | 0.223 ± 0.002 |
| ERA5 | 20736 | 41.161 ± 0.640 | 7.034 ± 0.055 | 0.198 ± 0.008 | 0.501 ± 0.001 |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

### Shallow Water Equations (SWE) Observations
*   **Impact of Sparsity on Standard EnSF:**
    *   The gradient of the log-likelihood function vanished in dimensions where observations were missing.
    *   Increasing observation sparsity (from full to $4\times$ to $225\times$ reduction) caused strictly increasing assimilation errors and slower convergence for EnSF (with 20 ensemble members).
    *   At $225\times$ reduction, standard EnSF RMSE did not decrease over time, even with dense temporal updates (every step).
    *   Increasing the ensemble size from 20 to 1000 for standard EnSF at $225\times$ sparsity resulted in decreasing errors, attributed to more accurate prior score estimation.
*   **Latent-EnSF Performance:**
    *   Latent-EnSF achieved small relative errors and fast convergence even at $225\times$ sparsity.
    *   Performance levels were comparable to standard EnSF operating with full-state observations.
    *   Latent-EnSF outperformed Latent-LETKF, Latent-EnKF, and Vanilla LETKF in terms of assimilation speed and accuracy across tested noise levels (0%, 10%, 20%).
    *   Visual reconstruction showed Latent-EnSF successfully corrected a perturbed initial state to match the ground truth, whereas EnSF failed, leaving the state near the perturbed baseline.
*   **Temporal Sparsity Robustness:**
    *   Latent-EnSF maintained accuracy when observation intervals increased (5, 20, and 50 time steps), showing only a slight increase in burn-in time.
    *   Latent-LETKF was sensitive to temporal sparsity, exhibiting significantly slower convergence as sparsity increased.
*   **Latent Space Analysis:**
    *   The difference between encoded true states and encoded noisy observations showed a stable standard deviation across time steps with a mean near zero.
    *   A latent scaling parameter ($\psi_{\text{latent}} = 20$) successfully mitigated numerical instability caused by small-scale variables in the latent space.

### ERA5 Weather Forecasting Observations
*   **Baseline Performance:**
    *   The FourCastNet model without data assimilation showed increasing accumulated errors over time, becoming unreliable after approximately 14 days.
    *   Standard EnSF with sparse ($64\times$) observations failed to correct the trajectory, yielding errors that closely tracked the "No DA" FourCastNet baseline.
*   **Latent-EnSF Performance:**
    *   Latent-EnSF quickly leveled off errors within the first few days and preserved accuracy throughout the 41-day window.
    *   Latent-LETKF resulted in increasing assimilation errors over time, significantly higher than Latent-EnSF.
*   **Role of Dynamical Model:**
    *   Comparison between "Latent-EnSF" (using FourCastNet) and "Latent-EnSF No Model" (assuming static state) confirmed that the ML-based forecasting model contributed to assimilation accuracy, despite its long-term drift.
*   **Variable-Specific Performance:**
    *   Assimilation for Z500 (geopotential height) was more accurate than for U500 (wind component).
    *   The U500 variable exhibited higher state complexity with sharp local changes, suggesting a need for denser observations than the $18 \times 9$ grid used.

### Computational Efficiency Analysis
*   **Scalability:**
    *   Latent-LETKF computational cost increased approximately linearly with dimension.
    *   Latent-EnKF computational cost exploded with dimension (taking over 700 times longer for ERA5 than SWE).
    *   Latent-EnSF demonstrated high scalability, taking only ~4 times longer for the higher-dimensional ERA5 task compared to the SWE task, despite a ~50x increase in latent dimension.
*   **Speed:**
    *   Latent-EnSF was faster than standard EnSF in the full space, even accounting for the overhead of the encoder/decoder forward passes.
    *   Latent-EnSF was the fastest method among all comparators for the high-dimensional ERA5 experiment (0.198s vs 7.034s for Latent-LETKF and 41.161s for Latent-EnKF).

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex

\begin{center}
%\framebox[4.0in]{$\;$}
\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}

\caption{Sample figure caption.}
\end{figure}
```

### Example Code for Tables
```latex

\label{sample-table}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

#### Anonymity Requirement
The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.  
Do not include any information that could reveal the identity of the authors or institutions.

#### Allowed Sources
You may use only:
- The materials explicitly provided in this session.
- Logical reasoning derived from those materials.

#### Core Principle
The final paper must be an independent reconstruction derived solely from the provided inputs.  
This constraint is strict and overrides all other instructions.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Accurate modeling of complex physical systems—such as weather forecasting or fluid dynamics—requires integrating observational data into Partial Differential Equation (PDE) or Machine Learning (ML) models, a process known as data assimilation. While traditional methods like the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) suffer from the "curse of dimensionality" in high-dimensional state spaces ($d \gg 1$), the recently developed Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) offers a promising alternative by leveraging score-based diffusion models to sample from posterior distributions.

However, a critical technical gap exists in the current EnSF formulation. In practical applications, observations are highly **sparse** ($y_t \in \mathbb{R}^m$ where $m \ll d$). When the observation map restricts information to a small subset of dimensions, the gradient of the log-likelihood function, $\nabla_x \log P(y_t | x_t)$, vanishes in the unobserved dimensions. This vanishing gradient prevents the EnSF from effectively updating the state in unobserved regions, rendering the method ineffective for real-world sparse data scenarios. We aim to solve the joint challenge of high-dimensional state estimation and high-sparsity observations.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **Latent-EnSF**, a novel architecture that performs data assimilation within a compressed latent space rather than the full state space. Our core hypothesis is that by training a **coupled Variational Autoencoder (VAE)** with dual encoders, we can map both the high-dimensional full state and the sparse observations into a consistent, low-dimensional latent representation.

By aligning these representations, we transform the sparse observation problem into a full-rank problem within the latent space. This allows the latent observation map to be approximated as an identity function, thereby preventing the vanishing gradient issue. We hypothesize that performing score-based diffusion sampling in this regularized latent space will enable accurate reconstruction of the full posterior state, maintaining the benefits of EnSF while overcoming its sparsity limitations.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Coupled VAE Architecture
We will construct a coupled VAE framework consisting of two distinct encoders and a shared decoder.
*   **State Encoder ($\mathcal{E}$):** Maps the full state $\boldsymbol{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ to a latent distribution parameters $\xi_t = (\mu_t, \sigma_t^2) \in \mathbb{R}^{2r}$.
*   **Observation Encoder ($\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{obs}}$):** Maps the sparse observation $\boldsymbol{y}_t \in \mathbb{R}^m$ to latent distribution parameters $\zeta_t = (\mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}, (\sigma_t^{\mathrm{obs}})^2) \in \mathbb{R}^{2r}$.
*   **Shared Decoder ($\mathcal{D}$):** Reconstructs the full state from the latent variable $z \in \mathbb{R}^r$ back to $\mathbb{R}^d$.

The latent variables are parameterized via the reparameterization trick:
$$ z_t = \mu_t + \sigma_t \cdot \epsilon_t, \quad z_t^{\mathrm{obs}} = \mu_t^{\mathrm{obs}} + \sigma_t^{\mathrm{obs}} \cdot \epsilon_t $$
where $\epsilon_t \sim N(0, I)$.

### 2. Consistency Optimization
To ensure the latent representations of the full state and the sparse observations are consistent, we will minimize a compound loss function $\ell_t(\theta)$. This loss will enforce reconstruction accuracy, alignment between the two encoders, and KL-divergence regularization against a standard normal prior $\nu = N(0, I_r)$.

We define the loss as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_t(\theta) = & \lVert x_t - \mathcal{D}(z_t) \rVert_2^2 + \lVert x_t - \mathcal{D}(z_t^{\mathrm{obs}}) \rVert_2^2 \\
& + \lVert \mathcal{E}(x_t) - \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{obs}}(y_t) \rVert_2^2 \\
& + \lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\nu_t \lVert \nu) + \lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\nu_t^{\mathrm{obs}} \lVert \nu)
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\theta$ represents the network parameters, $\nu_t$ and $\nu_t^{\mathrm{obs}}$ are the distributions defined by the encoders, and $\lambda$ is a weighting parameter (set to $10^{-5}$).

### 3. Latent Dynamics and Observation Maps
We will perform the Bayesian filtering update steps entirely within the latent space.
*   **Latent Dynamics:** The evolution of the latent state $\xi_t$ is approximated by encoding the evolution of the full dynamics:
    $$ \xi_t \approx \mathcal{E}(M(\mathcal{D}(z_{t-1}(\xi_{t-1})), \varepsilon_t)) $$
*   **Latent Observation:** Because the encoders are trained to align $\mathcal{E}(x_t)$ and $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{obs}}(y_t)$, we approximate the latent observation map as an identity function with additive noise $\hat{\gamma}_t$:
    $$ \zeta_t \approx \xi_t + \hat{\gamma}_t $$
    This approximation allows us to compute the likelihood gradient without automatic differentiation through the decoder, significantly accelerating the process.

### 4. Latent Diffusion Sampling (The Update Step)
We will implement the update step using a score-based diffusion model on the latent variable $\xi$. The diffusion process is defined by a reverse-time Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE):

$$ d\xi = [f(\xi, \tau) - g^2(\tau) \nabla_\xi \log P_\tau(\xi)] d\tau + g(\tau) d\bar{w} $$

where $\tau \in [0, T]$ is the diffusion time, $f$ is the drift term, and $g$ is the diffusion coefficient. We will define the posterior score $\nabla_\xi \log P(\xi_{t,\tau} | \zeta_{1:t})$ as:

$$ \nabla_\xi \log P(\xi_{t,\tau} | \zeta_{1:t}) = \nabla_\xi \log P(\xi_{t,\tau} | \zeta_{1:t-1}) + h(\tau) \nabla_\xi \log P(\zeta_t | \xi_{t,\tau}) $$

Here, $h(\tau)$ is a damping function (e.g., $1-\tau$). The first term (prior score) is estimated via Monte Carlo sampling from the ensemble. The second term (likelihood score) utilizes the identity approximation derived in Section 3, ensuring non-vanishing gradients.

To handle numerical instability in the compact latent space, we will introduce a scaling factor $\psi_{\mathrm{latent}}$ (e.g., $\psi_{\mathrm{latent}}=20$) to rescale latent representations before applying the diffusion process.

### 5. Algorithm Execution
The proposed execution flow for one time step $t$ is:
1.  **Encode:** Convert prior ensemble $\{x_{t-1}\}$ to latent priors $\{\xi_{t-1}\}$ and observation $y_t$ to latent observation $\zeta_t$.
2.  **Propagate:** Evolve latent priors via the approximate latent dynamics to obtain predicted latent ensemble $\{\xi_t\}$.
3.  **Diffuse:** Solve the reverse-time SDE from $\tau=T$ to $0$ to generate posterior latent samples, utilizing the gradient of the latent likelihood.
4.  **Decode:** Map the posterior latent samples back to the full state space: $x_t = \mathcal{D}(z_t)$.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Solution to Sparse Observation Failure:** By mapping sparse observations to a full-rank latent vector, we theoretically eliminate the vanishing gradient problem inherent in standard EnSF, enabling its use in real-world sparse data scenarios.
2.  **Computational Efficiency:** The assimilation process (solving the SDE) occurs in a reduced dimension $2r \ll d$. We expect this to significantly reduce computational cost compared to high-dimensional particle filters or standard EnSF.
3.  **Unified Representation:** The coupled VAE provides a mathematically consistent framework for handling heterogeneous data sources (full state models vs. sparse sensors) within a single probabilistic manifold.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
